newsitem.title: FRANCE: Gaullist militants' caution follows jubilation.
newsitem.headline: Gaullist militants' caution follows jubilation.

text.p: Fired-up Gaullist militants shouted themselves hoarse with delight on Sunday night when they heard the first projected results from the opening round of France's general election..

But rythmic chants of "On-a-gagne, On-a-gagne," (Weve won, weve won) soon gave way to a slightly modified "On-va-gagne" (We're going to win) when they realised the results were much less heartening than they first thought.

Several hundred supporters packed two large tents set up outside their campaign headquarters on Avenue George V, half-way between the Champs Elysees and the Crazy Horse night club, home of super-elegant strippers.
The militants waited anxiously for eight p.m. when large television screens, set up in the tents, began broadcasting the first projected results.

A great cry of "Ouayyyyy" went up when projections showed the combined list of the Gaullist Rally for the Republic (ROR), to which most of those present belong, and the Union for French Democracy (UDF) was credited with 31 to 37 percent of votes, the only list to exceed 30 percent.
"We're France's biggest party," exulted burly Gilbert Edelstein, director of the Pinder-Jean Richard circus and a veteran of three decades of Gaullist political campaigns.
"This shows the French are intelligent, that we don't always throw away something good which we've just started to build," he boomed as cameras zoomed in on him.
Many began enthusiastically jostling their way towards a huge buffet table laden with mouthwatering sausages, cheeses and fine Bordeaux and Burgundy wines.
Some present soon realised, however, that while no single left-wing list equalled that of the government backers, the total of left-wing votes was about equal, if not superior, to that of the right.

For parliamentarian Andre Santini, one of the rare UDF leaders present: "It's true, the French have sent us a warning. It's up to us to show them before the second round (next Sunday) that we have heard them."

Rank-and-file militants however had no doubt about the final outcome: "The French people have chosen reason over dreams (by the left) or over dividing the country (the extreme-right) and we will win," confidently predicted 22-year-old student Pierre.

Puffing clouds of smoke from a pipe which could well have belonged to his father, Pierre and his business school friend Alexei, 20, looked typical of a new breed of Gaullist party workers widely represented in the tent.

Clad in three-piece business suits and accompanied by immaculately-coiffed girlfriends in expensive designer clothes, the eager youths appeared to be a self-appointed class of future parliamentarians.

As they buttonholed slightly puzzled foreign reporters, an older breed of Gaullists was clustered around the buffet, perspiring profusely and wolfing down camembert sandwiches, chased down by glassfulls of red wine.

A disappearing breed, these worker-class Gaullists, in their 50s and 60s, looked uneasily about them. One man, his nose and cheeks now nearly as red as the wine he drank, sighed: "Ah. things have certainly changed since the days of the General (de Gaulle)."
